newsitem.title: UK: UK tobacco industry determined to fight ad ban.
newsitem.headline: UK tobacco industry determined to fight ad ban.

text.p: The tobacco industry on Thursday sharply criticised the British government's plans to publish a draft bill to ban tobacco advertising and said it is determined to fight for the right to continue to advertise a legal product.

"We're not resigned to it," Clive Turner, executive director of industry affair's for Britain's Tobacco Manufacturers Association, told Reuters on Thursday in a phone interview. "We are not going to put a defeatist face on it. We believe we have extremely sound, rational arguments, and we want to present them."
Turner said TMA wrote to Public Health Minister Tessa Jowell requesting a meeting on the proposed ad ban.
"We do feel we've got a right, even a responsibility, to make ourselves heard before the government makes an irrevocable decision or finalises its plans," Turner said.
"We want to know why the government thinks it's necessary to introduce legislation, and ask why they are doing this when it won't make a difference on consumption," he added.

Britain's Advertising Association, a federation of 27 trade and professional groups, said the government move was expected and it welcomed further chance for consultation on the draft bill. But Lionel Stanbrook, deputy director general, said that while any monetary impact on the advertising industry would be small, the ban sets a poor precedent.

"I hope it will not prove to be the first in a line of dominoes and give a green light to people who think our public interest agenda is so overwhelming in its sincerity that this means we can go ahead and ban Mars bars and chocolate cakes," Stanbrook said.

Spokesmen for British tobacco makers Rothmans (UK) Ltd and Gallaher Ltd said their companies are opposed to the proposed ban and hope to talk to the government. Rothmans, Gallaher and Imperial Tobacco are the largest tobacco makers supplying the UK market.
Imperial chief executive Gareth Davis on Wednesday said the government should agree to voluntary restrictions instead of a statutory ban.

Existing restrictions on tobacco advertising, including a ban on television and radio advertising and restrictions on how cigarettes are portrayed in other advertising media, all operate under a series of voluntary agreements.
Government officials on Wednesday said the government was determined to carry through its commitment to an advertising ban during the current session of parliament, which will last until late 1998.
According to the TMA, UK consumers spent about 12 billion stg ($19.7 billion) on tobacco products in 1996, and the industry spends about 53 million pounds on advertising in newspapers and billboards.

AC Nielsen Meal, a media research firm, said tobacco companies in 1996 spent 46.6 million stg on press advertising in the UK. The firm said it had no details on the amount spent on billboards, because the tobacco industry and poster contracters will not to disclose those figures.
Gallaher and Imperial declined to disclose their advertising budgets.
